value.hook: Open before adding a destructive sweep with brakes, an in-memory guard around a revive/spawn/launch, a DeliveryFailure variant, or when a mutant survives a test that seems to cover it
value.title: F276 (#332): retiring a dead seat's queue; a guard's lifetime follows the operation's owner

sections.name: body
sections.value:
F276 (#332, merged): the 60 s park-notice sweep fails, at most 64 per pass, the open delivery:/delivery-control: jobs of seats tombstoned more than 7 days ago, as undelivered:recipient-retired (an ordinary park, so live senders hear and dead ones don't). Live AFTER: 345 retired, 32 spared, 15 notices, no duplicates.

What the next coder should know:

1. A guard's lifetime follows whoever owns the operation, not whoever asked for it (B332-01, my round-1 BLOCK). The revive intent lived in the HTTP handler. Since R309-01 the launch outlives a cancelled request and still writes the row, so the guard ended early. Fix: SpawnHold::carry, so the launch task owns it until the row write or a failure. Before you hold anything in a handler, ask what keeps running after the request is gone (launch_seat_locked spawns its own task).

2. Test brakes through the real entry point, and cancel it. My first revive tests took the intent directly, so they could never see B332-01. The working harness: real registry, queue and spine via crate::build_services; FakeTmux; a Registry wrapper that latches put_lifting_owner_close; spawn revive::revive_seat from http::tests, abort it at the latch, then sweep. See a_cancelled_revive_spares_its_seats_queue_until_its_launch_writes_the_row.

3. When a mutant survives a test that seems to cover it, look at the path the test actually drives. My dead-sender mutant survived because the sweep only notices LIVE seats' parks, so notify's guard was never reached. The live follower is what calls notify on every published park. Hand the park to notify directly.

4. A new DeliveryFailure variant must also go into the TS PARKED_OUTCOMES (.omp/extensions/pij/adapters/rust-runtime.ts). A contract test pins it equal to the Rust wire vocabulary, and an unknown failed outcome throws "needs a recognized outcome". Rust peek_parked is a different list (inbox snapshot and recovery) and deliberately omits some outcomes.

5. Dry-run destructive work on a copy (sqlite3 -readonly ~/.pij-rs/pij.sqlite ".backup …"; rm -f copy* first, because a stale -wal corrupts it). Then run the REAL code on a second copy in a throwaway test, so the PR's counts are the code's counts.

6. Tooling trap: my mutant helper ran `git checkout -- <file>` to restore a file after writing its patch, and it wiped my uncommitted edits twice. Commit before generating mutants. Regenerate any patch whose context moved after fmt or a rebase (`git apply --check` every patch).

7. A main squash of a stacked PR can be byte-identical to the head you tested on. Check with `git diff <tested-base> <main>`, and if it's empty, cite it rather than re-running everything. `harness checks` DID pass locally (15/15) after `just worktree-deps` in a fresh worktree.
